PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations

Travis Davies    Wentao Ma    Lihao Guo    Tengfei Ma    Xiaowen Chang    Jiafeng Xu    Shilong Wang    Yiqi Deng    Shaowen He    Xiaoqi Li    Qian Zhu    Ran Cheng    Hao Dong Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Email: travisdavies@qiyuan-robot.com
Abstract

A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action–frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

1 Introduction

A world model that renders the consequences of a policy’s actions can serve as a simulator: rollouts become parallel, repeatable, and free of the risk of damaging hardware. This sidesteps both the danger and the sample cost of online training on real hardware [43, 64, 65, 61], and avoids the sim-to-real gap [34, 19] and the per-environment engineering that hand-built physics simulators demand. The idea runs from model-based reinforcement learning, where agents learn from imagined rollouts alone [30, 31, 32, 79], through interactive video generation for games and open-ended worlds [4, 7, 23, 73, 55, 66, 20], to action-conditioned robot world models [29, 25, 50, 26]. What such a model must do is narrower than generating plausible video: it must adhere to the actions a policy issues, keep several camera views consistent, and stay coherent over rollouts far longer than the window it was trained on. We present PrimeSim, a world model built as a robot simulator that meets all three requirements.

To enable faithful action following and consistent multiview generation, we adapt a pretrained video model to robot dynamics through midtraining on 30,110 hours of demonstrations spanning 22 robot platforms. For action following, we unify heterogeneous robot controls into a shared action representation and introduce frame-aligned dual-path action conditioning, combining temporally aligned attention with direct action injection to establish precise correspondence between robot controls and generated motion. For multiview consistency, we introduce view-aware interleaved attention, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving camera-specific representations through explicit camera identities. Through joint conditional flow-matching training, these designs allow a single model to learn action-conditioned, multiview robot dynamics across diverse embodiments, establishing the foundation for an interactive world model simulator.

While midtraining establishes action-conditioned multiview generation within a fixed temporal window, turning the model into a practical robot simulator introduces a fundamental challenge: autoregressive simulation requires continuously conditioning on the model’s own imperfect predictions, whereas conventional video generators are trained on fixed-length, ground-truth contexts. This mismatch leads to error accumulation over extended rollouts and is compounded by the computational cost of iterative video generation. To address these challenges, we develop a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that progressively transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient, long-horizon autoregressive simulator. First, we enable fast generation through chunk-causal adaptation and four-step consistency distillation, making sequential simulation and subsequent self-rollout training computationally tractable. Second, we improve self-conditioned stability through self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching against the frozen bidirectional teacher, allowing the model to learn from its own generated histories rather than relying solely on ground-truth context. Third, we introduce hierarchical temporal memory to support long-horizon coherence, preserving the initial scene, sparse long-term history, and dense recent motion within a bounded KV cache. Together, these components enable efficient autoregressive simulation that remains robust to self-generated context and scales beyond the original training window.

Together, these designs enable PrimeSim to generate temporally coherent rollouts up to 105 seconds at 10.1 FPS, supporting diverse robotic manipulation tasks involving both rigid and deformable objects. Compared with five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim achieves state-of-the-art performance on WorldSimProbe [16], leading four of its five suites: global trajectory coverage by 10.0%, action-source behavior preservation by 41.8%, and interaction dynamics by 48.4%, each measured against the strongest competing model on that axis, with interaction grounding also led at 85.7. On EWMBench, PrimeSim reaches the best overall score of 6.09, ahead of both GE-Sim variants (5.82 and 5.79) and every instruction-conditioned model, and is best on five of the eight dimensions, including perfect scores on high-level semantics, trajectory alignment and logical consistency, with action semantics (BLEU) 72.7% above the strongest GE-Sim variant. Beyond benchmark fidelity, we demonstrate the practical utility of PrimeSim as a learned simulator for GRPO-based policy optimization [27], enabling policy improvement through model-generated interactions. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code to support further research.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that transforms a pretrained video generator into an interactive robot world model through a progressive midtraining and posttraining framework.

  • •

    We develop a large-scale midtraining framework using 30,110 hours of demonstrations across 22 robot platforms. With unified cross-embodiment action representations, frame-aligned dual-path conditioning, and view-aware interleaved attention, PrimeSim learns action-faithful and multiview-consistent robot dynamics across diverse embodiments.

  • •

    We introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that combines efficient causal generation, self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching, and hierarchical temporal memory. This enables fast, self-conditioned autoregressive simulation while mitigating long-horizon error accumulation beyond the original training window.

  • •

    We demonstrate strong performance across diverse rigid and deformable object manipulation tasks: 10.1 FPS at four sampling steps, coherent rollouts of up to 105 seconds, 6.09 overall on EWMBench (first), and first on four of five WorldSimProbe suites against five open-source action-conditioned world models, retaining the lead on two of the three action-realisation axes and interaction dynamics. We further validate PrimeSim as a learned simulator for GRPO-based policy optimization.

2 Data Engine

Our goal for training data was to learn from a massive and diverse pool of settings while keeping our representations simple. To this end, we assembled 30,110 hours of robot demonstration data from a mix of open-source and proprietary sources. Dataset statistics are shown in Fig. 3, and an overview of the datasets used is provided in Table 12. In general, we include any demonstration data that can be converted into our unified format with reasonable effort, whether humanoid, dual-arm, single-arm, UMI [14], or simulated. We describe the conversion pipeline, quality filtering, and dataset composition below and in the appendix.

Robot Data Pooling.

Motivated by the low cost of data collection, recent state-of-the-art methods pretrain on large egocentric human videos with a smaller ratio of robot data [45, 25, 83]. However, aligning robot actions to latent actions or predicted hand-to-end-effector poses adds additional complexity. Since pooled robot datasets, open- and closed-source together, now largely match the scale of the egocentric corpora those models relied on, we skip the alignment problem entirely: we train directly on robot demonstrations from both sources and simply unify their action and state spaces using the general action representation described in Sec. 3.2.1.

Dataset Staging.

Each training stage serves a different purpose, so each should be trained on a different data distribution. For midtraining, we require vast and highly diverse data sources, so we use the entire dataset. For posttraining, the model has already seen the full corpus and the stage mainly aims to improve long-horizon and real-time responsiveness rather than to broaden coverage. We therefore train it on small datasets collected for specific downstream tasks, which are long enough to contain complete episodes and representative of what the deployed simulator is asked to continue, rather than on a subsample of the pretraining mixture.

2.1 Data Pipeline

2.1.1 Stage 1: Video Quality Filtering

Spatiotemporal validity.

We discard clips whose motion or temporal characteristics fall outside the corpus distribution. Motion is assessed via dense optical flow [22]: given the flow field 𝐮t​(p)\mathbf{u}_{t}(p) between adjacent frames, we compute

M⁡(V)=1T−1​∑t=1T−11|Ω|​∑p∈Ω‖𝐮t​(p)‖2,M(V)=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{p\in\Omega}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}(p)\|_{2}, (1)

where Ω\Omega is the image domain. The motion score is not used to retain only high-motion samples; instead, it supports distribution control. Near-static clips are downsampled so the corpus is not dominated by a small number of platforms that remain stationary. Motion scores are read within a platform rather than across the corpus, because the flow a camera records at rest varies markedly between fixed, handheld and wrist-mounted views. The retained data therefore spans subtle in-hand manipulation, camera movement, and larger end-effector displacement without collapsing toward either motion extreme.

Artifact detection.

We remove frames and clips containing JPEG encoding artifacts, and discard any whose state or action values are numerically corrupted.

Episode length filtering.

Clips shorter than 1 second are excluded, as they do not provide enough temporal context for autoregressive training.

2.1.2 Stage 2: Action Quality Filtering

Embodiment-type filtering.

Datasets with dexterous hands or humanoid legs represent a small fraction of the pooled corpus. To keep the action representation simple, we filter these datasets out. This removes legged locomotion, not humanoids as a class: humanoid platforms on a wheeled chassis are kept, because their arm, torso and chassis commands all fit the slots the interface already provides, and they supply the largest single share of the corpus (Fig. 3).

Anomaly detection.

We discard sequences whose action signals contain discontinuities inconsistent with continuous robot motion. We detect these as outliers in the first difference of each action channel: an isolated step change far outside the distribution of adjacent steps indicates a sensor or logging fault rather than a commanded acceleration. Datasets containing corrupted video frames, or action values outside their admissible range, are discarded as well.

Missing action detection.

Some datasets leave certain action features blank, such as end-effector pose or chassis velocity. If these values cannot be recovered through forward kinematics, the affected data is dropped.

2.1.3 Stage 3: Data Alignment

Frequency alignment.

We preserve each dataset’s native sampling rate at collection time, but resample to a fixed 10 Hz during training. If a dataset cannot be resampled to exactly 10 Hz within a 0.03 s timestamp tolerance, we use the closest achievable frequency.

Camera alignment.

The number of cameras varies across embodiments. To make batches collatable, we fix the model’s camera count to three. Datasets with more than three cameras have their uncommon cameras dropped; datasets with fewer have the primary camera repeated until three slots are filled.

Prompt alignment.

Datasets differ in whether they provide natural-language task descriptions. For datasets that include prompts, we keep them as is. For datasets that do not, we generate a prompt from the task metadata with a template-based generator, so that every training sample is paired with a task description.

Format conversion.

All datasets are converted to LeRobot [8] format. We chose this format for three reasons: (i) its storage is space-efficient, (ii) many open-source datasets already use it, and (iii) recent updates have made it reliable for large-scale training at the tens-of-thousands-of-hours scale used in this project.

2.1.4 Stage 4: Action Alignment

End-effector unification.

Datasets store end-effector pose inconsistently, and we unify it in three steps. For datasets that provide joint-space commands without end-effector poses, we look up the robot’s open-sourced URDF and compute them using the forward kinematics implementation in LeRobot [8]. For datasets with poorly defined action labels, we discard the labels and use proprioceptive data instead, taking the pose one timestep ahead as the current timestep’s action. Rotations vary across datasets in both parametrization and quaternion component ordering, so we convert every rotation to a matrix and then to a quaternion in (x,y,z,w)(x,y,z,w) order, with the real value last. Datasets lacking both end-effector poses and usable joint-space commands are excluded.

PrimeSim action unification.

To unify actions across heterogeneous embodiment platforms, we convert every action into a shared representation consisting of bimanual end-effector poses with quaternion rotations, full-body joint angles, gripper commands, and chassis velocity in (vx,vy,ω)(v_{x},v_{y},\omega). Gripper commands are binary open/close signals and are kept in absolute form. We refer the reader to Sec. 3.2.1 for the full specification.

Relative action chunk.

We convert absolute actions into relative action chunks by expressing every action in the coordinate frame of the proprioceptive state at frame 0 of the current window. For body joints, we take the difference between the current joint configuration and the reference configuration,

q~t=qt−q0.\tilde{q}_{t}=q_{t}-q_{0}. (2)

For end-effector pose, we express the current translation and rotation in the reference frame. Let pt∈ℝ3p_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and Rt∈S​O​(3)R_{t}\in SO(3) denote the end-effector translation and rotation at time tt, and let p0,R0p_{0},R_{0} denote their values at the reference frame. The relative pose is

p~t\displaystyle\tilde{p}_{t} =R0⊤​(pt−p0),\displaystyle=R_{0}^{\top}(p_{t}-p_{0}), (3)
R~t\displaystyle\tilde{R}_{t} =R0⊤​Rt.\displaystyle=R_{0}^{\top}R_{t}. (4)

Equivalently, in homogeneous form, T~t=T0−1​Tt\tilde{T}_{t}=T_{0}^{-1}T_{t} where Tt=[Rt∣pt]T_{t}=[R_{t}\mid p_{t}]. Gripper commands and chassis velocity are left unchanged, as both are already expressed in a frame-independent form.

3 PrimeSim

PrimeSim aims to serve as a world model simulator for long-horizon robot manipulation, generating future camera observations conditioned on robot actions. Unlike conventional video generation, robot simulation requires the model to faithfully execute prescribed actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and preserve coherent scene dynamics over extended trajectories. Moreover, the simulator must support low-latency autoregressive generation to enable efficient interaction with robot policies.

To address these requirements, we adopt a progressive training framework that transforms a pretrained video generator into an action-conditioned, multiview, autoregressive simulator. We first initialize PrimeSim from a pretrained video generation backbone that provides general visual and motion priors. During midtraining, we introduce structured action conditioning and multiview adaptation to learn robot dynamics from large-scale demonstrations. During posttraining, we progressively adapt the model for causal generation, few-step sampling, and long-horizon self-conditioned rollouts with persistent temporal memory.

3.1 Pretrain

We initialize from the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B pretrained weights [75], which provides a strong generative prior over natural video: object permanence, lighting and material statistics, and short-horizon motion patterns that would be prohibitively expensive to relearn from robot data alone. This stage establishes the general world priors, spatiotemporal coherence and high-fidelity texture that the later stages build on. We adopt this checkpoint as given: all of our own training happens in the midtraining and posttraining stages that follow.

3.2 Midtrain

Midtraining adapts the pretrained video generator to action-conditioned robot dynamics. While the pretrained backbone provides general visual and motion priors, it lacks explicit control over robot actions and consistent generation across multiple camera views. To address these limitations, we introduce three complementary components: a unified cross-embodiment action representation, frame-aligned dual-path conditioning, and view-aware interleaved attention. We jointly train these components with the video generation backbone on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms (Sec. 2).

Problem Formulation.

Our objective during midtraining is to learn the visual consequences of prescribed robot actions across multiple camera views. At robot timestep tt, let ot=(𝐈t,qt)o_{t}=(\mathbf{I}_{t},q_{t}) denote the observation, where 𝐈t=(It1,…,Itn)\mathbf{I}_{t}=(I_{t}^{1},\ldots,I_{t}^{n}) contains images from nn cameras and qtq_{t} represents the robot’s proprioceptive state.

Given an observation context 𝒪t=(ot−K+1,…,ot)\mathcal{O}_{t}=(o_{t-K+1},\ldots,o_{t}), an HH-step action trajectory At=(at+1,…,at+H)A_{t}=(a_{t+1},\ldots,a_{t+H}), and an optional language instruction ℓ\ell, we formulate multiview video prediction as

𝐈t+1:t+H∼𝒲BD(⋅∣𝒪t,At,ℓ),\mathbf{I}_{t+1:t+H}\sim\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{BD}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{O}_{t},A_{t},\ell), (5)

where 𝒲BD\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{BD}} denotes the bidirectional world model learned during midtraining. Unlike autoregressive simulation, the model jointly predicts the future video within a fixed temporal window. This formulation provides the foundation for the action and multiview conditioning mechanisms described below.

3.2.1 Action Representation

We define actions as changes in robot poses. Given consecutive video tokens, an action token ata_{t} denotes the pose change that produces the transition into latent frame tt. Each embodiment source is transformed into a fixed 31-dimensional representation that captures a shared underlying geometric structure across different action domains, with the slots an embodiment lacks set to zero.

General Action Representation.

At a high level, actions can include up to four components: effector poses for the agent’s effectors, grasp states, pose of the head, waist, and torso, and the chassis velocity. To cover manipulation poses across almost all robot platforms’ pose representation, we represent arm states as end-effector poses, grasp states as binary flags, head/torso/waist as joint angles, and the chassis as a planar velocity (vx,vy,ω)(v_{x},v_{y},\omega). As each embodiment’s degrees of freedom varies, we leave redundancy in each joint slot to account for this (see Fig. 5).

Relative Action Chunk.

All actions are defined relative to the initial frame of each window, i.e., a~t+i|t=at+i⊖at\tilde{a}_{t+i\mid t}=a_{t+i}\ominus a_{t}. This relative action representation for conditioning resolves several core issues in cross-embodiment learning. First, embodiments with missing features can simply be represented as 00 (no movement). Second, the absolute origin offset of each embodiment is cancelled out by the relative transformation. Third, it strengthens the per-frame action conditioning signal by grounding all changes to the conditioning first frame, as well as concentrating the action distribution. Relative actions have been explored in prior models, but with deltas taken from the previous frame [25]. We argue that anchoring to the first conditional frame of the window instead provides a stronger conditioning signal for world models. An ablation for relative action chunk is provided in Table 9.

3.2.2 Action Conditioning

Effectively controlling a world model to generate future frames that faithfully follow commanded actions remains a fundamental challenge. Existing models often hallucinate robot motions inconsistent with the conditioned actions [13, 67]. We attribute this limitation in part to the lack of explicit temporal alignment between actions and generated frames. Under standard global attention, each frame can aggregate action information from multiple timesteps, making it difficult to identify which action should govern its evolution. To address this, we introduce a frame-aligned dual-path conditioning mechanism, which strengthens action–frame correspondence by explicitly binding actions to their corresponding frames through two complementary pathways. while the second directly injects action information into frame representations, ensuring that action conditioning does not rely solely on attention routing. Together with our first-frame-anchored relative action representation, these designs provide temporally precise and explicit control over generated robot motions. We evaluate their individual contributions in Table 10.

Action Tokenizer.

To enable frame-aligned conditioning, we first establish a temporal correspondence between robot actions and video latents. Specifically, we encode each relative action chunk into a compact sequence of latent action tokens using a two-layer MLP, producing one action token for each latent video frame. This representation provides a shared temporal structure for the two conditioning pathways described below, allowing each frame to be associated with the action responsible for its evolution.

Framewise Action-Conditioning.

Given the aligned action tokens, our first conditioning pathway explicitly constrains how actions interact with video representations. Rather than allowing every frame to attend to actions from arbitrary timesteps, we introduce a shifted-diagonal attention mask that restricts frame-to-action attention to the corresponding temporal transition. Specifically, since action ata_{t} drives the transition into frame t+1t+1, frame tt attends only to at−1a_{t-1}, while the initial conditioning frame receives no action conditioning. This prevents interference from temporally unrelated actions and establishes an explicit action–frame correspondence at the attention level. While prior work has explored frame-level action conditioning [29], our approach enforces this correspondence directly through the attention mask and combines it with first-frame-anchored relative action chunks, which specify the intended motion relative to a consistent reference state.

Action-Frame Adapter.

Although framewise attention establishes which action each frame should attend to, it does not guarantee that the corresponding action signal sufficiently influences the frame representation. In particular, action information may still be underweighted when competing with rich visual features during attention. We therefore introduce a complementary conditioning pathway that directly injects the aligned action information into each frame token. Specifically, a lightweight action–frame adapter computes a residual feature shift from the corresponding action token and integrates it into the frame representation (Figure 4). Unlike attention-based conditioning, this pathway provides a direct route for action information, independent of the learned attention weights. The two pathways thus serve distinct but complementary roles: framewise attention determines which action governs each frame, while the adapter ensures that the selected action directly modulates its representation. Their combination strengthens action–frame binding and encourages generated motions to remain consistent with the specified action trajectory.

3.2.3 Multiview Adaption

A fundamental challenge in action-conditioned multiview generation is ensuring that different camera views remain consistent with the same evolving physical scene. This is particularly challenging in robotics, where wrist-mounted cameras move with the robot and may observe one another, creating strong dependencies across views. Treating each view independently can lead to inconsistent robot motions and object interactions, while unrestricted global attention may obscure view-specific information. To address this, we introduce view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, which enables cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations.

Specifically, we organize the 30 DiT blocks to alternate between intra-view and global attention: two out of every three blocks restrict attention to tokens within each camera view, while every third block enables information exchange across all three views. This design allows the model to capture view-specific spatial and temporal relationships locally, while periodically integrating information across cameras to maintain a coherent representation of the shared physical scene.

However, effective cross-view interaction also requires the model to distinguish the source of each visual token, particularly when features from different cameras are mixed through global attention. We therefore prepend a dedicated camera token to each view, explicitly encoding its view identity throughout the generation process. The two designs serve complementary roles: interleaved attention controls how information is exchanged across views, while camera tokens preserve which view each representation belongs to. Together, they promote consistent multiview generation without sacrificing view-specific information (Figure 4). We validate the contribution of both components in Table 11.

3.2.4 Training Objective

Having established the unified action representation, frame-aligned action conditioning, and view-aware multiview attention, we jointly optimize these components under a conditional latent flow-matching objective. Rather than introducing separate objectives for action following or multiview consistency, both capabilities are learned through the conditional generation of future multiview observations.

Let x0=ℰ(𝐈t+1:t+H)x_{0}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{I}_{t+1:t+H}) denote the clean latent representation of the target multiview video, where ℰ\mathcal{E} is the video encoder. We collect the conditioning inputs as c=(𝒪t,At,ℓ)c=(\mathcal{O}_{t},A_{t},\ell), comprising the observation context, action trajectory, and optional language instruction.

For a sampled flow timestep τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] and Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}), we construct the noisy latent and its target velocity:

xτ=(1−τ)​x0+τ​ϵ,vτ=ϵ−x0.x_{\tau}=(1-\tau)x_{0}+\tau\epsilon,\qquad v_{\tau}=\epsilon-x_{0}. (6)

The conditional velocity network uθBDu_{\theta_{\mathrm{BD}}} is trained to predict the target velocity:

ℒflow​(θBD)=𝔼(x0,c),ϵ,τ​[‖uθBD​(xτ,τ,c)−vτ‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}(\theta_{\mathrm{BD}})=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{0},c),\epsilon,\tau}\left[\left\|u_{\theta_{\mathrm{BD}}}(x_{\tau},\tau,c)-v_{\tau}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (7)

where θBD\theta_{\mathrm{BD}} denotes the parameters of the bidirectional world model, and τ\tau indexes the generative flow process rather than robot time.

Importantly, all camera views are generated jointly, and robot actions are incorporated directly into the velocity prediction network through the proposed conditioning mechanisms. This allows the model to learn action-conditioned visual dynamics and cross-view dependencies under a unified generative objective.

The resulting bidirectional world model 𝒲BD\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{BD}} provides the foundation for subsequent autoregressive adaptation. During posttraining, we retain flow matching for initial causal adaptation, while introducing consistency distillation and distribution matching to enable efficient, self-conditioned, long-horizon simulation.

3.3 Posttrain

Midtraining equips PrimeSim with the ability to predict action-conditioned, multiview robot videos within a fixed temporal window. However, accurate short-horizon generation does not by itself yield a practical world model simulator. The midtrained model generates clips with bidirectional attention and requires many denoising steps, whereas policy interaction calls for continuously extending a rollout from the model’s own predictions. This introduces three additional challenges: autoregressive generation must respect temporal causality, sampling must be fast enough for repeated rollouts, and errors and missing scene context must not accumulate uncontrollably over long horizons.

We therefore posttrain PrimeSim to transform fixed-window video prediction into fast, self-conditioned, long-horizon simulation. Our guiding principle is fast video, slow memory: generate each new chunk with few-step sampling while retaining informative history across much longer timescales. We realize this through four progressive stages: (1) causal adaptation enables chunk-wise autoregressive generation; (2) consistency distillation produces a four-step sampler; (3) clip-level self-rollout with asymmetric distribution matching improves generation conditioned on the model’s own outputs; and (4) episode-level adaptation combines self-rollout training with bounded, multiscale temporal memory. The stages are sequential: causal generation enables rollout, fast sampling makes rollout training tractable, and self-conditioned training prepares the model for long-horizon continuation.

3.3.1 Stage 1: Autoregressive Modelling

To enable continuous simulation, we first adapt the bidirectional model 𝒲BD\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{BD}} obtained from midtraining into a chunk-causal model 𝒲C\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{C}}. Unlike the midtrained model, which jointly generates all frames within a fixed temporal window, the causal model generates video chunks sequentially, conditioned on previously generated observations. We achieve this through chunk-causal attention, which preserves bidirectional attention within each chunk while restricting cross-chunk attention to preceding chunks. This allows the model to retain its learned action-conditioned multiview generation capabilities while supporting autoregressive prediction.

Specifically, we adopt teacher forcing [36, 18, 9, 101, 85] during causal adaptation, where each chunk is conditioned on clean ground-truth history. Let Bi,cleanB_{i,\mathrm{clean}} and Bi,noisyB_{i,\mathrm{noisy}} denote the clean and noisy representations of chunk ii, respectively. The attention context for each noisy chunk is defined as

𝒮⁡(Bi,noisy)={Bj,clean:j<i}∪{Bi,noisy},\mathcal{S}\!\left(B_{i,\mathrm{noisy}}\right)=\left\{B_{j,\mathrm{clean}}:j<i\right\}\cup\left\{B_{i,\mathrm{noisy}}\right\}, (8)

where 𝒮⁡(⋅)\mathcal{S}(\cdot) denotes the accessible attention context. This design prevents information leakage from future chunks while allowing all chunks to be trained in parallel. The same chunk partition also determines the noise granularity of the diffusion-forcing objective. Stage 1 therefore keeps the flow-matching loss of Eq. 7; what changes is the attention mask the loss is evaluated under, which is what we mean by diffusion forcing rather than a new objective.

Through this adaptation, PrimeSim acquires the ability to generate future observations autoregressively rather than within a fixed bidirectional window. However, teacher forcing introduces an exposure bias: the model is trained with clean historical observations but must condition on its own imperfect predictions at inference. Increasing the chunk size from k=1k=1 to k=3k=3 reduces the number of sequential generation chunks from nine to three in our training window, mitigating but not eliminating error accumulation. To enable subsequent training on self-generated histories, we first reduce the computational cost of autoregressive generation through few-step distillation in Stage 2.

3.3.2 Stage 2: Causal Consistency Distillation

Although Stage 1 enables autoregressive generation, the resulting causal model 𝒲C\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{C}} still requires 50 denoising steps per chunk, making continuous simulation computationally expensive. More importantly, the high sampling cost makes it impractical to train on self-generated rollouts, where gradients must propagate through multiple generation chunks. To address this, we adopt Causal Consistency Distillation (Causal CD) [97] to obtain an efficient four-step generator. Specifically, we use 𝒲C\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{C}} as a frozen causal teacher and initialize a causal student 𝒲θ\mathcal{W}_{\theta} from its weights. Both models share the same chunk-causal architecture, allowing the student to preserve the autoregressive structure learned in Stage 1 while substantially reducing the number of sampling steps.

Rather than supervising the student with complete teacher-generated trajectories, Causal CD performs online distillation by matching local transitions of the teacher’s flow trajectory. Let xtx_{t} denote a noisy video latent at flow time tt, x^0,C\hat{x}_{0,\mathrm{C}} the teacher’s clean estimate, and xt−Δ​tCx_{t-\Delta t}^{\mathrm{C}} the target obtained from a local teacher ODE step. The distillation objective is

ℒCD​(θ)=𝔼xt,t,Δ​t​[w⁡(t)​d​(Gθ​(xt,x^0,C,t),xt−Δ​tC)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{t},t,\Delta t}\left[w(t)\,d\!\left(G_{\theta}(x_{t},\hat{x}_{0,\mathrm{C}},t),x_{t-\Delta t}^{\mathrm{C}}\right)\right], (9)

where GθG_{\theta} denotes the student’s local flow-map update and d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) measures the discrepancy between student and teacher transitions. By matching nearby flow states, the student learns to approximate the teacher’s multi-step generation process with substantially fewer sampling steps. Moreover, the online objective requires only a local teacher ODE step per update, avoiding the expensive precomputation and storage of complete teacher trajectories.

To further reduce the memory overhead of maintaining teacher and student models simultaneously, we optimize LoRA [33] adapters while keeping the midtrained backbone weights frozen. Together, these designs produce a four-step causal student that substantially accelerates autoregressive generation and, crucially, makes self-rollout training computationally tractable. Nevertheless, distillation alone does not resolve the exposure bias inherited from teacher-forced training, nor does it guarantee visual fidelity under repeated self-conditioned generation. We therefore further optimize the distilled student on its own generated rollouts in Stage 3.

3.3.3 Stage 3: Clip-Level Self-Rollout with Asymmetric DMD

Although Stage 2 substantially accelerates autoregressive generation, the distilled student 𝒲θ\mathcal{W}_{\theta} still faces two limitations. First, training with clean historical observations introduces exposure bias, as the model must condition on its own imperfect predictions during inference. Second, consistency distillation has a forward-KL-like, mode-covering effect, potentially producing averaged predictions with reduced perceptual detail. To address both limitations, we introduce clip-level self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching. Specifically, the student autoregressively generates video chunks within each training clip, with subsequent chunks conditioned on its own previously generated latents through the causal KV cache, rather than on ground-truth history. This exposes the model to the conditioning distribution encountered during inference.

To preserve generation quality under self-conditioned rollouts, we further optimize the student using an asymmetric Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) objective [90, 89]. Unlike Stage 2, which distills a causal teacher into a causal student, we now use the frozen bidirectional model 𝒲BD\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{BD}} from midtraining as the reference teacher. This design exploits the stronger fixed-window generation capability of the bidirectional model to supervise the autoregressive student, without imposing the teacher’s bidirectional attention structure on the student. We adopt the mode-seeking reverse-KL objective

DKL(pθ(⋅∣c)∥pBD(⋅∣c)),D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c)\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{BD}}(\cdot\mid c)\right), (10)

where pθp_{\theta} and pBDp_{\mathrm{BD}} denote the conditional distributions of the causal student and bidirectional reference model, respectively, and cc represents the corresponding conditioning information, including visual context, robot actions, and camera-view identities.

To optimize this objective, we introduce a trainable fake-score network vϕv_{\phi} that estimates the distribution of student-generated samples. Together with the frozen bidirectional reference, it provides the score difference used to update the student. Let x~0\tilde{x}_{0} denote the clean video latent generated by the student, and let x^0,ϕ\hat{x}_{0,\phi} and x^0,BD\hat{x}_{0,\mathrm{BD}} denote the clean-sample estimates of the fake-score network and bidirectional teacher, respectively, evaluated on the same noisy latent. We construct the normalized score-difference direction as

∇KL=x^0,ϕ−x^0,BDmax⁡(𝔼​|x~0−x^0,BD|,δ),δ=10−8,\nabla_{\mathrm{KL}}=\frac{\hat{x}_{0,\phi}-\hat{x}_{0,\mathrm{BD}}}{\max\!\left(\mathbb{E}\left|\tilde{x}_{0}-\hat{x}_{0,\mathrm{BD}}\right|,\delta\right)},\qquad\delta=10^{-8}, (11)

where the normalization stabilizes the update when the student’s generated distribution deviates substantially from the reference. The student is optimized using the surrogate loss

ℒgen​(θ)=12​‖x~0−sg⁡(x~0−∇KL)‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\tilde{x}_{0}-\operatorname{sg}\left(\tilde{x}_{0}-\nabla_{\mathrm{KL}}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}, (12)

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes the stop-gradient operator. Meanwhile, the fake-score network is trained on student-generated samples using the standard flow matching objective,

ℒcritic​(ϕ)=𝔼x~0,ϵ,τ​[‖vϕ​(xτ,τ,c)−(ϵ−x~0)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{critic}}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x}_{0},\epsilon,\tau}\left[\left\|v_{\phi}(x_{\tau},\tau,c)-(\epsilon-\tilde{x}_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (13)

where xτ=(1−τ)​x~0+τ​ϵx_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\tilde{x}_{0}+\tau\epsilon is the noisy interpolation of the generated latent, and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I).

Through clip-level self-rollout and asymmetric distribution matching, Stage 3 enables the four-step causal student to learn from its own generated history while receiving high-quality supervision from the bidirectional reference. However, training remains confined to fixed-length clips, whereas practical robot simulation requires coherent generation over complete episodes. This remaining short-training–long-inference gap motivates the episode-level self-rollout and persistent temporal memory introduced in Stage 4.

3.3.4 Stage 4: Episode-Level Long-Horizon Adaptation

While Stage 3 enables self-conditioned generation within short clips, reliable robot simulation requires maintaining coherent predictions over trajectories far longer than the training window. At this scale, two challenges become particularly critical: prediction errors accumulate as generated chunks repeatedly serve as future conditioning, and important scene information may be lost from recent context due to occlusion or camera motion. To address both challenges, we extend self-rollout training from fixed-length clips to complete robot episodes and introduce a persistent hierarchical temporal memory. The former exposes the model to long-horizon error accumulation during training, while the latter preserves scene information across multiple temporal scales. Together, they enable the student to generate extended trajectories using its own predictions rather than relying on clean historical observations.

Stage 4 inherits the asymmetric DMD objective of Stage 3 unchanged. What changes is what the rollouts span: the student is now supervised on episodes rather than fixed clips, so the distribution it is matched against includes the errors it accumulates over a long horizon rather than only over a few chunks.

Episode-level self-rollout.

We first extend self-conditioned generation to complete robot episodes, allowing the student to experience the long-horizon conditioning distribution encountered during inference. Specifically, the student generates successive video chunks autoregressively, with each continuation conditioned on its own previously generated history through the causal KV cache. Generator gradients are accumulated across the episode, followed by a single optimization update at the episode boundary. Meanwhile, the fake-score network is updated after each generated window to track the evolving student distribution. The KV cache persists throughout the episode and is reset only when a new episode begins. Unlike clip-level training, this procedure directly exposes the student to errors that accumulate across successive generations, encouraging more stable long-horizon predictions.

Memory in world models is usually conditioned on encoded ground-truth observations [29, 63, 50, 67] or on a cache of clean historical frames [86, 92, 81]. Both supply, at inference, data the model does not itself produce, which opens a train-inference gap. PrimeSim instead trains its memory on its own rollouts, so the distribution it conditions on during training is the one it will have at inference.

Hierarchical temporal memory.

Although episode-level self-rollout exposes the model to longer trajectories, it does not by itself prevent the loss of historical information. Retaining every generated frame is computationally expensive, while keeping only recent frames can discard important scene states. We therefore introduce a hierarchical temporal memory that organizes the KV cache into three complementary components: global sink, slow memory, and local memory.

The global sink retains the initial observed latent state as a persistent reference throughout the episode. The local memory stores recent consecutive generated latents, preserving fine-grained motion information. The slow memory, in contrast, maintains a sparsely sampled representation of longer-term history. After each generation window, the previous local-memory entries are merged with the existing slow-memory bank and temporally downsampled to a fixed capacity, while the newly generated latents populate the next local-memory bank. Temporal positions are preserved during downsampling, and synchronized frame indices are used across all camera views to maintain aligned multiview histories.

This hierarchical design allows each generated chunk to access the initial scene, sparse long-term context, and dense recent motion within a bounded memory budget. Importantly, except for the initial observed state, all memory entries originate from the student’s own generated history. The same memory update mechanism is used during training and inference, avoiding the distribution mismatch introduced by teacher-forced historical context.

Latent-space continuation.

To further improve the efficiency and consistency of long-horizon generation, we maintain the student’s continuation entirely in latent space. Rather than decoding each generated segment and re-encoding it as a new conditioning observation, the student carries its history forward through the persistent KV cache. Continuation windows receive neither a new first-frame latent nor a clean ground-truth prefix, ensuring that the autoregressive process remains conditioned on the model’s own predictions. This avoids repeated video decoding and encoding along the generation path and allows the student to extend trajectories without repeatedly reinitializing visual context.

Amortized supervision.

A remaining challenge is supervising episode-length student rollouts using the bidirectional reference and fake-score networks, which operate within fixed temporal windows. We decouple long-horizon generation from local distribution supervision. For each continuation, we decode the preceding segment once and re-encode only its final frame as a conditioning observation for the score networks, as required by the causal VAE. This operation is performed outside the student’s gradient path, and the re-encoded observation is never fed back into the student’s autoregressive generation. Consequently, the student can accumulate history across complete episodes, while the score networks evaluate local transitions within their original temporal windows. This enables long-horizon self-rollout training without extending the temporal context of the supervising models.

Action re-anchoring.

Finally, to preserve consistent action conditioning across long rollouts, we express actions relative to the reference pose recorded at the beginning of each episode, rather than resetting the reference at every generation window. This maintains a consistent action coordinate frame across continuation boundaries and prevents changes in the reference frame from introducing ambiguity into the conditioned motion trajectory.

Together, the four posttraining stages transform PrimeSim from a fixed-window, action-conditioned video generator into a fast, self-conditioned, long-horizon world model simulator. Few-step distillation enables efficient autoregressive generation, while episode-level self-rollout and hierarchical temporal memory support coherent simulation across extended robot trajectories. At inference, PrimeSim requires only the four-step causal student and its bounded KV cache, generating future multiview observations conditioned on robot actions without access to ground-truth future frames.

4 Experiments

Six sets of experiments follow, in the order the paper’s argument develops. We first place PrimeSim against existing world models on benchmarks built for embodied prediction, together with the inference cost that decides whether a model can serve as a simulator at all. We then ask what midtraining actually acquires, by adapting to platforms and to scenes and camera placements the model has never seen. We examine what post-training changes over long horizons, whether the simulator is faithful enough to evaluate and to improve a policy, and finally which of the design choices carry the result.

4.1 Comparison to the State of the Art

We compare on three axes, chosen because a simulator has to be right about different things than a video generator. Trajectory fidelity asks whether the commanded motion is actually realised; scene and semantic consistency asks whether the world still looks and means the same while that motion happens; and inference cost asks whether the model can be run inside a control loop at all. WorldSimProbe separates the first two into its own axes, EWMBench aggregates them into a single score, and neither measures the third, so we report throughput separately.

4.1.1 WorldSimProbe Evaluation

WorldSimProbe [16] isolates a property that reconstruction metrics do not capture: whether a world model behaves as a simulator. It is built on the Observable Simulator Contract, which requires that supplied actions induce corresponding agent motion, and that the environment respond to that realized motion rather than to the action that was merely commanded. This targets a failure mode invisible to PSNR, in which the robot does not move as instructed while the scene reacts as though it had.

The benchmark decomposes the observable simulator contract into five diagnostic suites. T1 (Local Action Calibration) tests whether the model reproduces the simulator’s response to small and large action perturbations. T2 (Global Trajectory Coverage) evaluates whether it follows globally different but physically executable trajectories transferred across tasks and scenes. T3 (Action-Source Behavior Preservation) examines whether behavioral differences among expert, human-teleoperated, and policy-generated actions, such as speed, smoothness, and corrective motion, are retained. T4 (Interaction Grounding) uses validated no-contact counterfactuals to test whether the model avoids hallucinating interactions unsupported by the realized robot motion. T5 (Interaction Dynamics) assesses whether both robot motion and object response match intended interaction primitives such as pushing, pulling, rotating, shaking, and dropping.

We evaluate PrimeSim with a sink token that provides lightweight historical context for bidirectional architectures. To improve physical understanding, we additionally construct training data from three sources: multiple trajectories sampled from VLA task executions, perturbed variants of these sampled trajectories, and trajectories obtained after randomly replacing objects in the scene. Random visual noise is also applied during training to reduce the distribution shift caused by the mismatch between training and evaluation resolutions. PrimeSim generates 192×256192\times 256 images per view and predicts 33 frames at 10 FPS. Because the benchmark does not explicitly score appearance, task success, or coarse rollout-level responsiveness, the resulting comparison is primarily behavioral, and high scores indicate simulator fidelity rather than visual quality or downstream utility.

Against five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim ranks first on four of the five suites, leading two of the three action realization axes (T2 at 67.9 and T3 at 72.3) and interaction dynamics (T5 at 37.1). The one axis we do not win is informative rather than incidental. LingBot-VA leads local action calibration (77.0 against 70.2), indicating that our fine-grained control precision is not yet the best in the field even where coarse trajectory coverage is. Interaction grounding (T4) is led by us at 85.7 against Ctrl-World’s 77.5, and it follows from the same design decision read the other way: PrimeSim trains memory on its own rollouts rather than on encoded ground-truth observations, so the model learns the environment’s response to motion it actually produced, which is what this suite measures.

4.1.2 EWMBench Evaluation

EWMBench [93] evaluates embodied world models on eight dimensions covering scene consistency (SceneC), motion accuracy (HSD, Dyn and nDTW) and semantic alignment with the task instruction (BLEU, CLIP, Logics), plus a Diversity term across candidates. The overall score is the sum of the eight dimensions, each in [0,1][0,1]. We evaluate on the standard 21-episode community split across 7 AgiBot World [2] tasks (as used in [24]). For each episode we generate multiple rollouts under a fixed action-conditioned protocol, exploring a small family of sampler settings so that both fidelity and cross-sample diversity are represented; scores reflect EWMBench metric suite on these generations.

These episodes are in-domain: AgiBot World contributes to the training corpus, and the models compared here are fine-tuned from the midtrained checkpoint on these datasets before scoring. The EWMBench numbers therefore measure how well the architecture absorbs an in-domain benchmark rather than zero-shot transfer to it; Section 4.2 is where held-out platforms are evaluated.

PrimeSim rolls out open-loop at 10 FPS, conditioned on the first frame, the task instruction and the ground-truth action trajectory, in 33-frame windows chained over the episode. Videos are generated at 192×256192\times 256, scored at the EWMBench frame size of 480×640480\times 640 on the head-camera stream against the 10 FPS ground-truth lane. These quality results use the multi-step sampling recipe (50 denoising steps, CFG 1.5), while the wall-clock latency numbers in Sec. 4.1.3 use the four-step distilled Stage-3 sampler.

As shown in Table 2, PrimeSim reaches an overall score of 6.09, exceeding the action-conditioned GE-Sim (LTX, 5.82) reported under the same metric accounting; the action-conditioned Thinker-WM variant stands at 5.03. The instruction- and text-conditioned field sits further below: EnerVerse-FT reaches 4.70 in the EWMBench paper’s own evaluation, the strongest recent embodied world models on the same 21-episode split, Thinker-WM (4.66) and Qwen-RobotWorld (4.60), cluster just under it, and the strongest general video models remain below 3.9. We emphasize that the second block of the table is not iso-protocol with ours, as those models condition on instructions or text rather than actions.

4.1.3 Inference Speed Comparison

We benchmark the wall-clock inference throughput of the four-step distilled PrimeSim against recent action-conditioned world models, with CausalWM included as a related text-conditioned generative reference.

Protocol.

All timings are measured on a single NVIDIA A100-80GB in bfloat16 at batch size one. The unit of work is one autoregressive chunk of future frames under each model’s released inference recipe, timed by wall clock with CUDA synchronization, including GPU-to-CPU materialization when it is part of the public API. Checkpoint loading, model construction and warm-up chunks are excluded, and we report steady-state means; per-model warm-up schedules and timing scopes are given in Appendix B. Because multi-view generators emit several RGB images per time step, we report two rates. Temporal FPS (TempFPS) counts rollout time steps produced per second. View-frame FPS (ViewFPS) counts each camera view as one frame and is our primary throughput metric: comparing only TempFPS would penalize a multi-view model, since each time step already renders VV images. For single-view models the two rates coincide; PrimeSim’s ViewFPS is three times its TempFPS.

Results.

Table 3 ranks the measured systems by ViewFPS. PrimeSim is fastest: 30.35 ViewFPS (10.12 TempFPS), rendering a 33-frame three-view window at 288×384288\times 384 in 3.16 s.

Among external systems the closest comparison is GE-Sim 2.0, which is also four-step distilled and three-view. It reaches 6.73 ViewFPS, 1.67×1.67\times the resolution- and horizon-matched BWM setting at 4.04 ViewFPS. Two published numbers are not comparable on this bench and we do not use them: GE-Sim 2.0 reports 10.9 Hz [63] and DreamDojo 10.81 FPS [25], both measured on H100 rather than A100, and DreamDojo’s distilled student weights were not public when we ran. BWM’s own configuration (672×896672\times 896, 48 frames) falls to 0.78 FPS, the clearest illustration of how strongly throughput depends on resolution and horizon.

Caveats.

The rows are not matched in resolution, horizon or denoising budget: PrimeSim and GE-Sim 2.0 use four-step distilled samplers, while the public BWM and Ctrl-World checkpoints run 50-step sampling. Few-step distillation is part of the released systems, so the comparison is between released inference recipes rather than matched compute. Ctrl-World generates at the lower native 192×320192\times 320 per view, and CausalWM is text- and first-frame-conditioned rather than action-conditioned. PrimeSim’s throughput also depends on rollout length: longer continuous-KV episodes measure 7.63 TempFPS as the KV cache grows, and we quote the short-window steady state. Finally, PrimeSim is timed at 288×384288\times 384 per view under the RoboTwin 2.0 [11] Stage-3 evaluation contract, whereas the quality results above use 192×256192\times 256 generations; the latency geometry is stated explicitly and is not shared with those tables. This benchmark covers world-model chunk generation only, not an end-to-end control loop with a policy.

4.2 What Midtraining Learns

Midtraining is where the model acquires its action interface: action conditioning and multiview coupling are introduced and trained over 20 dataset families and 22 robot platforms (Sec. 3.2). The question we ask here is what else that stage leaves behind. If cross-embodiment training yields transferable features rather than a fit to the training distribution, those features should survive transfer along three axes at once: to platforms the model has never driven, to scenes it has never seen, and to camera placements it has never been mounted at. All three survive, and the first does so at a cost low enough to change what adding a new robot means in practice: an action-following rollout within 100 to 200 gradient steps, where the pretrained backbone does not reach one at ten to twenty times the budget. At a learning rate of 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, two hundred steps move the parameters by roughly 10−210^{-2}, so this is a small amount of optimisation rather than a finetune to convergence. The comparison therefore tests what midtraining already provides, not how much can be recovered by fitting each new platform. The protocol is in Table 4. Posttraining is analysed separately in Sec. 4.3, because it changes how the model is run rather than what it has learned.

Embodiment Generalisation.

Midtraining and posttraining are designed to broaden the model’s coverage of embodiments and dynamics. We probe whether that coverage has in fact yielded transferable knowledge by asking what a new platform costs. We hold out three platforms from the 20 dataset families of our training corpus (Table 12): a single 7-DoF arm (xArm 7) drawn from Open X-Embodiment [17], a bimanual platform (ViperX 300, as used by ALOHA [98]) and the original Stanford UMI gripper [14]. Similar embodiments do appear in the corpus, through Franka in DROID [40] and RoboMIND [78], ALOHA-style simulation in RoboTwin 2.0, and the two UMI corpora, and that similarity is what gives cross-embodiment training something to transfer. It does not make adaptation automatic, however: the kinematics, camera mounting and data distribution all differ, so whatever transfers must be re-expressed for the new body, which is the gap a practitioner bridges when deploying to a new robot. UMI is the sharpest case, since other handheld grippers appear in pre-training while this device does not.

For each platform we finetune two initialisations under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at a batch size of 1. Neither receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters, so the only difference between them is the starting point: the midtrained model already carries the action-conditioning and multiview modules learned from our 30,110-hour cross-embodiment corpus (Sec. 3.2), whereas the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone must initialise those modules from scratch. To avoid penalising the baseline for this, we deliberately grant it ten to twenty times the finetuning budget of the midtrained model: 2000 steps against 100 to 200.

The midtrained model reaches an action-following rollout on all three platforms within 100 to 200 steps (Fig. 7). The pretrained backbone, at 2000 steps, does not: its generations are neither visually plausible nor action-controllable, remaining blurry and exhibiting no plausible movement or contact.

We read this as transfer rather than fast fitting, for three reasons. The optimiser is barely used: 200 gradient steps at a batch size of 1 draw 200 training windows from the recorded episodes, which is far too few to re-learn a platform. No run receives an embodiment identifier or an embodiment-specific parameter, so the gain cannot come from a lookup on which body is present. And the same gap appears on a single arm, a bimanual platform and a handheld device, which rules out an explanation tied to one kinematic structure. The baseline, given ten to twenty times the optimisation, never reaches the regime at all, so the difference is not one of budget. Taken together, these leave little room for an account that does not involve knowledge already carried in the weights. What they do not separate is corpus scale from the presence of an action interface at all: the baseline begins without one, so the two cannot be disentangled here, and we make no claim about which contributes more.

Scene and Camera-Pose Generalisation.

The 30,110-hour corpus spans a wide range of environments, and we ask whether that coverage transfers to a setting the model has never seen. We sample action trajectories and initial frames from the XVLA open-source dataset [100], which is held out of pre-training entirely. XVLA shares the AgileX Piper bimanual embodiment and includes clothes-folding tasks, so the robot itself is familiar; what differs is the camera configuration, the camera poses, and the setting as a whole. We generate multiview video conditioned on the sampled actions and assess it along three axes: action controllability, whether the arms follow the commanded trajectory; object-motion plausibility, whether the cloth deforms and travels as it should; and cross-view coherence, whether the head and both wrist views remain consistent with one another.

Zero-shot, PrimeSim controls the arms accurately and generates simple cloth motion faithfully, with quality degrading as the motion becomes contact-rich and the generated cloth state drifts from the commanded action. Table 5 makes that cost explicit: against a matched in-distribution baseline under an otherwise identical protocol, the model loses 3.97 dB PSNR and 0.105 LPIPS on XVLA. Finetuning for 200 steps at a batch size of 1 recovers most of the gap, in both the arm trajectories and the cloth deformation (Fig. 8). Seen platforms remain stronger than any transfer setting, which is the expected ordering and is the point: these results measure the cost of moving to a new platform, not a ceiling on what the simulator can generate.

The two results together say something more specific than that the model generalises. The same interface that carries to an unseen platform also carries to an unseen setting, with the task prompt but no embodiment identifier at inference. What transfers is therefore not a robot’s appearance but the mapping from actions to their visual consequences, which is what a simulator has to encode and what a video prior alone does not.

4.3 Posttraining Analysis

Posttraining turns the midtrained model into a causal autoregressive simulator through chunk-causal attention, few-step distillation and self-rollout training (Sec. 3.3). Posttraining primarily changes the model’s causal generation and conditioning behavior, so we evaluate both its short-horizon efficiency and fidelity, and its stability as the rollout horizon increases.

4.3.1 Distillation Efficiency and Short-Horizon Fidelity

Distillation serves two purposes in PrimeSim: it reduces inference latency for interactive simulation, and it shortens the gradient graph during rollout training, where backpropagating through 20 to 50 denoising steps does not fit on current hardware. Table 6 ablates the sampler on the same RoboTwin 2.0 held-out split, with throughput measured on a single A100. Relative to the 50-step causal Stage 1 teacher, the four-step Stage 3 model improves throughput by approximately 9.0×9.0\times; the measured rates for every stage and for the released model are in the table.

4.3.2 Long-Horizon Robustness

Episode-level adaptation.

To evaluate the final long-horizon adaptation stage, we directly compare Stage 3, which performs self-rollout training within fixed-length clips, with Stage 4, which extends training to complete robot episodes. Both models are evaluated on the same ten episode-level held-out RoboTwin 2.0 trajectories using identical initial observations and robot actions.

Each rollout is initialized from the first ground-truth RGB frame and subsequently conditioned only on the model’s own generated history. The evaluated trajectories contain 610–1,046 generated frames, corresponding to 61.0–104.6 seconds at 10 FPS, and include three synchronized camera views.

Table 7 reports both the average quality over the complete rollout and the degradation between the first and last complete 32-frame generation windows. For PSNR and SSIM, degradation is computed as the first-window score minus the last-window score; for LPIPS, it is computed in the opposite direction. Lower degradation therefore indicates better long-horizon robustness for all three metrics.

Memory configuration ablation.

We further compare rolling and hierarchical KV-cache organizations under the same long-horizon evaluation protocol. For rolling memory, the allocation denotes sink and rolling slots; for hierarchical memory, it denotes global, slow, and local slots.

Under the same 21-slot budget, hierarchical memory consistently outperforms the 3+183+18 rolling cache. It improves both average and final-window quality, while reducing Δ\DeltaPSNR from 8.427 to 6.008 dB, Δ\DeltaSSIM from 0.120 to 0.079, and Δ\DeltaLPIPS from 0.233 to 0.159. This supports separating persistent, long-term, and recent context within the KV cache.

4.4 PrimeSim as Policy Simulator

The video metrics in the preceding sections measure how closely PrimeSim reproduces recorded trajectories. For a policy simulator, the more relevant question is whether conclusions drawn inside it carry over to the real environment. We examine this in two ways: whether PrimeSim predicts and ranks the success rates of fixed policies as a physics simulator does (Sec. 4.4.1), and whether it can serve as the training environment for reinforcement-learning post-training of a policy (Sec. 4.4.2).

Setup.

We use the LIBERO-Spatial suite (10 tasks) in the LIBERO simulator as the reference, where success is LIBERO’s privileged-state task predicate. Policies are OpenVLA-OFT after supervised finetuning on LIBERO-Spatial demonstrations; they predict 8-step action chunks from the main camera view. Inside a world model, success is judged by a ResNet-based binary classifier finetuned on LIBERO-Spatial frames, which predicts from each generated frame whether the task has been completed; an episode receives a sparse reward of 1 if any of its frames is classified as success and 0 otherwise.

4.4.1 Policy Evaluation Fidelity

We first freeze the policy and ask whether the world model predicts its success rate. We take eight OpenVLA-OFT policies of clearly different competence, whose simulator success ranges from 29.3% to 85.0%. Each policy is run with greedy actions from the same 300 initial states (10 tasks ×\times 30 trials), once in the LIBERO simulator and once closed-loop inside the world model. As a reference world model we use a publicly released Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [75] finetuned on LIBERO-Spatial (Wan2.2-FT). We report the Spearman rank correlation ρ\rho and the Pearson correlation rr between world-model and simulator success, and the mean absolute gap |Δ||\Delta| between the two.

PrimeSim orders all eight policies exactly as the simulator does (Spearman ρ=1.00\rho=1.00, Pearson r=0.99r=0.99) and stays within 7.0 points of the simulator for every policy, with a mean absolute gap of 2.8 points (Fig. 9(a)). Wan2.2-FT also tracks the overall trend (r=0.91r=0.91) but mis-orders several policies (ρ=0.90\rho=0.90), and its errors grow with competence: it under-estimates the three strongest policies, whose simulator success is 79.0%, 82.0% and 85.0%, by 12.0, 12.7 and 18.3 points, for a mean absolute gap of 8.3 points. A world model that systematically under-rates good policies is of limited use for checkpoint selection, which is exactly where policy evaluation in a world model is needed.

4.4.2 RL Post-training inside PrimeSim

Beyond evaluation, PrimeSim can serve directly as the training environment for policy post-training. Starting from the SFT policy, we run GRPO (group size 8) entirely inside PrimeSim: rollouts are generated closed-loop by the world model and receive the sparse binary reward from the success classifier, and the physics simulator is never queried during training; it is used only to evaluate the resulting policy. After 200 RL steps, the policy’s success rate in the LIBERO simulator rises from 61.7% to 73.2%, and PrimeSim’s own estimate (60.1% to 71.9%) stays within 1.6 points of it (Fig. 9(b)), showing that improvements obtained purely inside PrimeSim transfer to the physics simulator.

Scope of this experiment.

The aim here is to show that PrimeSim supports RL post-training, not to maximise absolute success on LIBERO. We deliberately use a short training budget and an off-the-shelf success classifier, so the numbers measure whether closed-loop policy optimisation inside the model works at all, not what the best attainable score is. What longer optimisation would buy, and what it would risk, is discussed under limitations in Section 6.

4.5 Ablation Study

We run component ablations rather than stage comparisons. Action representation, action conditioning and multiview consistency each isolate one midtraining choice, and we train all three from the pretrained checkpoint rather than the midtrained one, so that the stronger priors midtraining already supplies cannot mask the contribution of the component under test. The distillation ablation is the exception, since post-training begins from the midtrained model by construction and its variants are therefore compared from that checkpoint. The midtraining ablations use a small in-house dataset collected for folding clothes on one humanoid embodiment.

This setup has a scope worth stating once rather than in every subsection. Each ablation below is run on a single embodiment, an in-house humanoid for some and the simulated RoboTwin 2.0 [11] setup for others, so the comparisons isolate how one component behaves within one kinematic frame; none of them measures cross-embodiment behaviour, and the platform adaptation results in Sec. 4.2 are the evidence that speaks to that. A mechanism whose value is specifically cross-embodiment, such as the relative action convention cancelling each robot’s absolute origin, has nothing to act on in either setting, so these numbers are more likely to understate such components than to overstate them.

4.5.1 Action Representation

We compare three ways of representing actions: absolute poses, delta poses relative to the previous frame, and our relative action chunk anchored to the first frame of the window. To isolate the effect of the representation itself, we initialize all variants from the pretrained checkpoint rather than the midtrained one, so the comparison is not biased by stronger priors learned during midtraining. Results are shown in Table 9, reported in PSNR [37], SSIM [77], and LPIPS [96].

4.5.2 Action Conditioning

We ablate our two action conditioning mechanisms, framewise action conditioning and the frame-action adapter, by applying each in isolation and then together. Because prior work [67, 39] also uses two-channel action conditioning but relies on standard cross-attention and AdaLN-zero [62], we compare each proposed channel against its conventional counterpart: framewise conditioning against vanilla cross-attention, and the token-level adapter against AdaLN. The final row tests both proposed channels together. Results are shown in Table 10.

Reconstruction metrics do not measure controllability, so we test action following directly. We evaluate on counterfactual actions, meaning action sequences that do not correspond to the recorded trajectory: faithful generation therefore requires the model to respond to the commanded motion rather than replay the recorded one. PrimeSim follows these out-of-distribution commands, as shown in Fig. 10, where static scene elements remain stable across the rollout while the commanded motion is carried out.

A qualitative figure cannot by itself settle whether the motion is genuinely action-driven, and we do not ask it to. WorldSimProbe provides the independent quantitative test, and its T3 suite, action-source behaviour preservation, asks precisely the counterfactual question: whether behaviour survives when the actions originate from a different source than the one that produced the video. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim ranks first on T3 (72.3) and on the coarse trajectory axis T2 (67.9), and second on local calibration T1 (70.2 against LingBot-VA’s 77.0) (Table 1). The two lines of evidence agree, and they agree on the residual weakness as well: action following holds at trajectory scale, while fine-grained local calibration is not yet the best in the field.

4.5.3 Multiview Consistency

The three views share one transformer stack rather than separate per-camera networks. Each of the 30 DiT blocks attends within its own camera view, and every third block instead spans all three, so relations inside a view are established before information is periodically integrated across views. A learned camera token marks which view each token belongs to.

We perform an incremental ablation of the multiview consistency mechanisms, introducing each component in turn to isolate its contribution. The baseline concatenates frames along the height dimension without any conditioning. We then add a view token that conditions each view, and finally apply intra-view attention across the frame tokens. Results are shown in Table 11.

4.6 Qualitative Results

We show rollouts that are easier to judge by eye than by metric, and that the quantitative sections do not otherwise cover.

First, a sequence isolates what the temporal memory buys under occlusion (Fig. 12).

A second sequence shows rollouts on deformable cloth, the material class where long-horizon coherence is hardest to maintain (Fig. 13).

Two further sequences give a qualitative view of the EWMBench generations behind Table 2 (Fig. 14).

5 Related Work

Video Generation in Robotics

Recent advances in general-purpose video generation [75, 15, 87] have catalyzed a growing body of work applying these models to robotics. One prominent direction leverages video generation for data expansion: by synthesizing diverse visual trajectories, these models augment limited teleoperation data, enabling broader coverage of environments, objects, and tasks [58, 99, 95, 47]. This mitigates a central bottleneck in robot learning—the scarcity of large-scale, diverse demonstrations. A complementary direction exploits the spatiotemporal physical understanding that video models acquire through large-scale pretraining. Rather than treating generated video merely as data, these works use the model’s internal representations as a backbone for action prediction and planning, demonstrating strong performance on downstream robotic tasks [57, 50, 46, 5, 10, 21, 41, 60, 88]. Together, these two lines of work reflect a broader shift: video generation models are evolving from passive data synthesizers into active components of the robot learning pipeline, serving simultaneously as sources of supervision and as engines of physical reasoning.

Interactive World Models

Closely related to video generation is the emerging area of interactive world models, in which generation is conditioned on and steered by actions [70, 26, 4, 73, 23, 55, 7, 66, 20]. Much of this work targets interactive video games, from early action-conditioned systems [4, 7] to more recent higher-fidelity, longer-horizon ones [23, 73, 66, 55, 20]. More recently, the paradigm has extended to robotics [63, 84, 29, 53, 49, 48, 76, 52, 39, 28, 69, 68, 72, 25]. These robot-centric models differ from their game-oriented counterparts along several axes: they emphasize multi-view consistency [63, 84, 29] rather than a single fixed viewpoint; they operate on continuous, physically grounded control signals [29, 53] rather than discrete symbolic inputs [4, 7]; and they prioritize geometric and physical consistency [49, 48, 76] over visual aesthetics and responsiveness [23, 66]. Their use cases also diverge: game-based models target entertainment and content creation, whereas robot-based ones serve as learned simulators providing synthetic feedback for action evaluation, policy learning, and planning [52, 39, 28, 69, 68, 72, 25].

6 Limitations and Conclusions

Limitations.

Our evaluation is broad but not exhaustive, and we prefer to state the gaps rather than let them be inferred. One concerns the model itself: PrimeSim generates at 192×256192\times 256 per view, so our claims concern simulator fidelity, whether actions are realized and the environment responds, rather than pixel-level realism, and we make no like-for-like visual fidelity comparison against models operating at higher resolution.

A further gap is a question of resources rather than of method. Adaptation to a new platform is few-shot, requiring 100 to 200 gradient steps on that platform’s own data, rather than zero-shot. We expect this gap to close with more midtraining GPU-hours, tighter alignment of each corpus’s action and state conventions, and a larger and more diverse corpus, since all three act on the same quantity that makes the interface transferable at all. We have not demonstrated it, and state it as an expectation rather than a result.

A final gap concerns scope, and it is the one we consider most important. Most of our quantitative evidence, and all of our closed-loop evidence, comes from simulation: the benchmark comparisons are on LIBERO, and policy training and evaluation inside PrimeSim are validated in simulation only. Our real-platform results establish that PrimeSim generates faithful video on real data, zero-shot on XVLA and after few-shot adaptation to xArm 7, ViperX 300 and a UMI gripper, and that it follows commanded action across the whole action space including chassis velocity. What they do not yet establish is the simulator role on physical hardware. Whether generated rollouts are faithful enough to stand in for simulator rollouts when improving a policy on a real platform remains open, and it is the direction we intend to pursue next.

Conclusions.

We presented PrimeSim, a world model that turns a video generation backbone into an action-conditioned, multiview, causal simulator of robot manipulation. A three-stage curriculum does the work: midtraining on a 30,110-hour cross-embodiment corpus, midtraining that introduces action and multiview conditioning, and posttraining that converts the model into a causal few-step autoregressive generator.
