The result conditions on actions and the task prompt, but on no embodiment identifier at inference. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim leads the WorldSimProbe axes that measure action realization at trajectory scale and interaction dynamics, and it reaches those results at 10.1 FPS through four-step distillation rather than the fifty steps the teacher requires. Its features transfer: three held-out platforms reach action-following rollouts within 100 to 200 gradient steps, where a general video prior given ten to twenty times that budget does not. We expect the combination of a large cross-embodiment corpus, an explicit action interface and a causal few-step sampler to be a practical route toward learned simulators that are fast and controllable enough to train policies inside.

.1 Corpus Composition

Our training corpus pools a large collection of open-source and proprietary robot demonstration datasets, listed in Table 12. Our guiding principle was to include all available data of reasonable quality and build a pipeline that converts heterogeneous sources into a unified format. Below we describe the conversion steps, the filtering criteria, and the final representation choices.

Our in-house data consists of teleoperation demonstrations collected on the AgiBot G2, AgiBot G2X, and PrimeBOT H2 humanoid platforms for household tasks such as laundry and room tidying.

Appendix A Training Details

A.1 Architecture Hyperparameters

A.2 Training Hyperparameters

We report the architecture and the midtraining configuration for PrimeSim. All downstream stages reuse the same optimizer, precision, and backbone unless noted elsewhere.

The architecture is initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [75] and retains its backbone dimensions. We add only some lightweight action conditioning modules and three learnable view tokens on top of the frozen text encoder, so the trainable parameter count is close to the backbone’s.

Midtraining uses a cosine-decayed learning rate with a short warmup and a small minimum learning rate, which we found necessary to avoid late-stage loss spikes on long training runs. The action classifier-free-guidance dropout is set to 0.1 to enable guidance at inference without retraining.

A.3 Distillation Hyperparameters

Stage 3 refines the causal consistency student of Stage 2 with the asymmetric DMD objective of Sec. 3.3.3. Three models take part. The teacher is the frozen bidirectional midtrained model and supplies the real-data score. The student is the causal few-step generator being distilled. The critic is initialised from the teacher and then trained with standard flow matching on the student’s own samples, so it tracks the distribution the student currently produces rather than the one the teacher defines. Only LoRA adapters are trained on the student, and the adapters are exported directly rather than as an EMA of the full weights, which is why the adapter rank appears in the table.

The critic is updated five times per generator update. It has to stay ahead of a generator that is itself moving, and an under-trained critic supplies a gradient that points at stale targets. The real guidance scale of 3.0 is applied to the teacher’s score, which sharpens the supervision the student is matched against; without it the teacher averages over modes and the student inherits that averaging. Both networks use the same learning rate, and the sigma shift is the resolution-dependent noise-schedule shift of the flow matching formulation. Because the surrogate loss is built so that its gradient is exactly Eq. 11, the KL objective carries no separate coefficient, and no balancing weight between the two losses appears in the table. Table 17 lists the settings used for every Stage 3 result reported in this work.

Appendix B Latency Benchmark Details

This appendix collects the protocol details behind Table 3: the timing environment, per-model warm-up and chunk semantics, the configuration of every measured system, and the latent-token proxy used for fairness discussion.

B.1 Environment and Timing Scope

The unit of work is one autoregressive chunk of future frames at each model’s native chunk size. The timed region covers the chunk generation call, including GPU-to-CPU materialization of outputs when it is part of the public API: model.step() including numpy conversion for GE-Sim 2.0, pipe() plus .cpu() on future frames for BWM, text/observation encoding, chain-of-thought sampling and VAE decoding with preloaded weights for CausalWM, and run_episode with checkpoint loading, text encoding and forward kinematics excluded for PrimeSim. Checkpoint loading, tokenizer/model construction and first-time CUDA kernel compilation are never timed; warm-up chunks absorb compilation and cache effects.

B.2 Warm-up, Repeats and Chunk Semantics

B.3 Per-model Configurations

PrimeSim Stage-3 (ours).

Wan2.2-TI2V-5B with Stage-3 asymmetric DMD, action-conditioned, continuous KV cache with local attention span 9. Three views at 288×384288\times 384, 33-frame windows (32 usable frames) under the RoboTwin 2.0 Stage-3 evaluation contract, four-step consistency sampler at sigmas (1000,750,500,250)(1000,750,500,250). Steady-state repeats measure 10.006, 10.011 and 10.329 TempFPS (mean 10.115, 3.16 s per window); a longer continuous-KV episode of about 72 model frames measures 7.63 TempFPS, and a cold-start run without warm-up measures 6.41 TempFPS — neither is used as the headline. Timed scope is run_episode with loading, text encoding and forward kinematics excluded.

GE-Sim 2.0.

Cosmos 2B with Pose Expert, released distilled checkpoint, action-conditioned with an episode band of intrinsics, extrinsics and trajectory. Three views at 384×512384\times 512, history 4, future 25, four-step distilled sampling with sigma schedule (1.0,0.9375,0.8333,0.625)(1.0,0.9375,0.8333,0.625), triton_rope enabled and Liger/SpargeAttention off. Twelve timed chunks follow three warm-up chunks; early chunks are noisy (9.78 s to 44.84 s), so the steady state is the mean of the last five, 11.15 s per chunk.

BWM, fair-aligned.

Wan2.2-TI2V-5B with action AdaLN (BLM checkpoint, step-12000), conditioned on absolute end-effector actions. Single view at 384×512384\times 512, history 4, future 25 (chunk of 29 frames total), 50-step sampling at CFG 1.0. Three timed chunks measure 6.23, 6.15 and 6.19 s (mean 6.19 s). The distilled BWM-fast weights were not publicly available at measurement time.

BWM, official configuration.

Vendor-default inference config: single view at 672×896672\times 896, history 9, future 48, 50-step sampling. Mean chunk time 61.71 s. Reported as the heavy vendor-default point rather than as a fair peer.

Ctrl-World.

SVD image-to-video UNet with CLIP text, conditioned on 7D actions. Three views stacked on the height axis into a 576×320576\times 320 canvas (192×320192\times 320 per view), history 6, future 5, 50-step sampling. Five timed chunks measure 5.76 to 5.80 s (mean 5.78 s).

CausalWM.

LTX-2.3 22B with Gemma-3-12B, generating a flow →\to pointmap →\to RGB chain-of-thought from text and a first frame — not action-conditioned. Single view at 480×640480\times 640, 25 future frames, four steps per chain-of-thought stage. Two timed chunks measure 39.23 and 36.72 s (mean 37.97 s), with weights preloaded and load time excluded.

B.4 Latent-token Proxy

For fairness discussion we estimate the number of latent tokens per forward as

#​tokens^≈V×(⌊Tlat−14⌋+1)×⌊H8⌋×⌊W8⌋,\widehat{\#\text{tokens}}\;\approx\;V\times\Big(\big\lfloor\tfrac{T_{\text{lat}}-1}{4}\big\rfloor+1\Big)\times\big\lfloor\tfrac{H}{8}\big\rfloor\times\big\lfloor\tfrac{W}{8}\big\rfloor, (14)

i.e. a spatial×\timestemporal compression grid in the style of Cosmos/Wan tokenizers (spatial stride 8, temporal compression ≈4\approx 4). This is a coarse grid proxy, not FLOPs.

PrimeSim’s proxy uses the 33-frame window (3×9×36×48=46,6563\times 9\times 36\times 48=46{,}656); the continuous KV cache bounds the attention span but does not change this per-window grid count, so it is not inflated to a memory-plus-future figure.
